name: Data and analytics
description: Event data, usage metering, reporting, dashboards.

groups.gg: Moksy or GG Money data design fact

cards.subject: A tracking plan
says: lists every event and property the product is meant to send
gives each tracked event an owner and a written meaning
is the document analysts check before trusting a new event
cards.use: need everyone to agree what an event means before it ships
not: is generated automatically and never needs maintaining

cards.subject: An event property
says: carries the context of an event such as the plan, page or item involved
lets one event name serve many cases without a new event for each
cards.use: want to record which product a purchase event was about
not: replace the need to name the event

cards.subject: A user property
says: describes the person rather than a single action
is stored on the profile and applies to every later event
holds attributes such as signup plan or country
cards.use: want to segment every event by the plan the user signed up on
not: changes meaning each time a new event is sent

cards.subject: Object-action naming
says: names events as a thing and what happened to it, such as invoice_sent
keeps event names consistent and easy to search
avoids vague names like click or action
cards.use: want event names that stay readable as the product grows
not: requires a separate event for every screen pixel

cards.subject: An event ID
says: is unique to one occurrence of an event
lets a retried delivery be recognised and counted once
is generated at the source rather than on receipt
cards.use: hear that a network retry may send the same event twice
not: changes every time the event is retried

cards.subject: An event timestamp
says: records when the thing happened rather than when it was received
should be stored in a single timezone, usually UTC
can differ from the received time when a device is offline
cards.use: must order events from a phone that was offline for an hour
not: is always identical to the time the server received it

cards.subject: Client-side tracking
says: sends events from the browser or app on the user's device
captures interface actions such as scrolls and clicks
can be lost to ad blockers and closed tabs
cards.use: need to record how people move around the interface
not: is guaranteed to reach the warehouse every time

cards.subject: Server-side tracking
says: sends events from the backend after the action has really succeeded
is not blocked by ad blockers or browser settings
is the safer source for facts such as completed payments
cards.use: need an event for a payment that must be counted exactly once
not: sees every scroll and hover on the page

cards.subject: Event schema versioning
says: adds a new version when the meaning or fields of an event change
stops old and new data being mixed under one name by accident
lets analysts filter on the version they understand
cards.use: must change what a field means without breaking old dashboards
not: silently redefines the field in place

cards.subject: A late-arriving event
says: reaches the warehouse after the period it belongs to has been reported
can change numbers that were already published
is why pipelines reprocess a recent window instead of trusting yesterday's totals
cards.use: see yesterday's total rise after it was reported
not: is always safe to discard

cards.subject: A metric definition
says: states exactly how a number is calculated, including its filters and period
is written down once and shared
stops two teams reporting different numbers from the same data
cards.use: find that two dashboards show different totals for the same name
not: is clear enough without being written down

cards.subject: An active user
says: is counted only after taking a qualifying action in the period
depends on which action the team chooses to qualify
gives a different count if the qualifying action changes
cards.use: must decide what counts as being active this month
not: is anyone who has ever created an account

cards.subject: A north star metric
says: is the single measure of the value customers get from the product
guides teams towards the same outcome
should move when customers get real value
cards.use: want the whole company aimed at one measure of customer value
not: is always revenue for the quarter

cards.subject: A leading indicator
says: moves before the outcome it predicts
gives time to act before results arrive
is often an early behaviour such as activation
cards.use: want an early warning that renewals may fall
not: is only known after the quarter closes

cards.subject: A lagging indicator
says: confirms an outcome after it has already happened
is accurate but arrives too late to steer
includes revenue and churn
cards.use: need the final confirmed result of last quarter
not: moves before customers change behaviour

cards.subject: A guardrail metric
says: is watched to make sure a change does not cause harm elsewhere
protects measures such as page speed, errors or support load
can block a launch even when the main metric improves
cards.use: want to ship a faster signup without raising refund requests
not: is the metric a team tries to maximise

cards.subject: Churn rate
says: is the share of customers lost in a period
needs a clear denominator such as customers at the start of the period
can be counted by customers or by revenue
cards.use: want the share of subscribers who cancelled this month
not: counts new customers gained

cards.subject: Retention rate
says: is the share of a starting group still active later
complements churn, so the two add to one for the same group
is usually read per cohort
cards.use: want to know how many of last month's signups are still active
not: measures how many new users joined

cards.subject: Customer lifetime value
says: estimates the total margin a customer brings over the whole relationship
depends on assumptions about retention
is compared with the cost of acquiring that customer
cards.use: must decide how much to spend winning a customer
not: is the revenue from the first month only

cards.subject: A semantic layer
says: defines metrics once so every tool computes them the same way
sits between the warehouse and the dashboards
lets analysts reuse a definition instead of rewriting it
cards.use: want every dashboard to share one definition of revenue
not: stores the raw events before any cleaning

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: warns that a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
explains why people game the number they are rewarded on
is a reason to pair every target with a guardrail
cards.use: see a team hit its target while customers are less happy
not: says that more data always improves a measure

cards.subject: Usage metering
says: counts what each customer uses so limits and bills can be correct
records usage per customer, per period and per resource
feeds both enforcement and invoicing
cards.use: need to bill customers for what they consume
not: only counts logins

cards.subject: A usage ledger
says: records each unit of consumption as its own row
is append-only, so history is never edited
can be summed to rebuild any customer's usage for a period
cards.use: need a durable record that supports disputes
not: keeps only the latest running total

cards.subject: A reversing entry
says: corrects a ledger by adding an opposite row instead of editing the old one
keeps the original mistake visible in the history
nets out the wrong amount when totals are summed
cards.use: find a wrong amount already written to an append-only ledger
not: overwrites the earlier row in place

cards.subject: A summary snapshot
says: holds a fast running total for the current period
is read on the hot path instead of summing the whole ledger
can be rebuilt from the ledger if it drifts
cards.use: need a quick check of how much quota is left
not: is the source of truth for money

cards.subject: An idempotency key
says: is sent with a request so a repeat can be recognised
makes a retried write count once
is stored with the result of the first attempt
cards.use: retry a usage write after a timeout without double counting
not: makes every retry count again

cards.subject: Quota reservation
says: sets aside expected usage before the work is done
stops concurrent requests from jointly overspending
is followed by a commit of the actual amount
cards.use: must stop two simultaneous requests overspending the same allowance
not: is done only after the provider call returns

cards.subject: Quota commit
says: records the actual usage after the work finishes
releases any reserved amount that was not used
replaces the earlier estimate with the real figure
cards.use: want the final measured amount recorded after the call
not: happens before any work starts

cards.subject: A hard limit
says: blocks further use once the allowance is spent
gives the customer a firm cap on spend
needs a clear message so users know why they were blocked
cards.use: must guarantee a customer cannot exceed the plan
not: lets usage continue and bills the extra

cards.subject: Overage billing
says: allows use beyond the allowance and charges for the excess
avoids interrupting customers at the limit
needs the customer to agree to the extra price in advance
cards.use: want customers to keep working past their allowance and pay for it
not: blocks use at the limit

cards.subject: A billing period
says: is the span of time one allowance and one invoice cover
sets the date an allowance resets
must be computed from the right start date to avoid drift
cards.use: need to know when this month's allowance restarts
not: is always the calendar month

cards.subject: A dashboard
says: shows chosen measures on one screen for a given audience
is only useful if its numbers are trusted
should answer a question the viewer actually has
cards.use: want a quick view of how the business is doing
not: is finished once the charts look good

cards.subject: A single source of truth
says: is the one agreed place a number comes from
stops teams quoting different totals
is the dataset every report reconciles to
cards.use: find three reports quoting three revenue figures
not: is a copy of the data kept in each team's spreadsheet

cards.subject: A refresh timestamp
says: tells viewers how old the numbers are
is shown on the dashboard itself
helps explain why a figure differs from live data
cards.use: hear 'is this number current?' from a viewer
not: is hidden to keep the page tidy

cards.subject: Variance against plan
says: shows the gap between actual and planned figures
turns a bare number into a judgement
is clearer when the plan's history is kept
cards.use: want to know if revenue is ahead or behind target
not: is the same as the average of actuals

cards.subject: Drill-down
says: lets a viewer move from a total to the parts that make it up
helps explain why a number moved
relies on the detail rows adding up to the total
cards.use: need to find which region caused a drop in the total
not: hides the underlying detail

cards.subject: Self-serve analytics
says: lets non-analysts explore data without writing queries
depends on well-defined shared metrics
can produce conflicting numbers if definitions are not governed
cards.use: want business teams to answer simple questions without waiting on an analyst
not: removes the need for any data governance

cards.subject: Row-level security
says: limits which rows a viewer can see based on who they are
lets one dashboard serve many teams safely
is enforced in the data layer rather than by hiding charts
cards.use: need regional managers to see only their own region in one shared report
not: is achieved by hiding columns in the chart

cards.subject: Reconciling a total to source
says: compares a report's total with the system it was built from
catches missing rows and double counting
should be done before a new report is trusted
cards.use: build a new report and want proof its numbers are right
not: is only needed once a year

cards.subject: Completeness
says: asks whether required values are all present
is measured as the share of rows with the field filled in
fails when a form field is silently skipped
cards.use: find that a third of signups have no country
not: asks whether values are correct

cards.subject: Accuracy
says: asks whether a value matches the real world
cannot be proved by format checks alone
is checked by comparing with a trusted source
cards.use: suspect recorded prices differ from the invoices
not: asks only whether the field is filled in

cards.subject: Validity
says: asks whether a value fits the allowed format or range
catches an age of 400 or a malformed date
can pass even when the value is wrong
cards.use: need to reject a date written as 31/02/2026
not: proves a value matches reality

cards.subject: Consistency
says: asks whether the same fact agrees across systems
fails when one system says active and another says cancelled
is checked by comparing two sources of the same record
cards.use: find that billing and the CRM disagree on a customer's plan
not: asks whether the data is up to date

cards.subject: Timeliness
says: asks whether data is fresh enough for its use
is measured as lag between an event and its availability
matters more for operational alerts than for annual reports
cards.use: hear that the dashboard is a day behind and ops needs hourly
not: asks whether values are in the right format

cards.subject: Uniqueness
says: asks whether each real thing appears once
fails when a customer has two records
is the aim of deduplication
cards.use: find the same customer listed three times
not: asks whether the field is filled in

cards.subject: A null value
says: means a value is missing or unknown
is not the same as zero or an empty string
is skipped by most aggregate functions
cards.use: need to tell 'no answer' apart from 'answered zero'
not: is identical to the number zero

cards.subject: Data lineage
says: traces a number back through each step to its source
shows which reports a change would affect
helps find where an error entered
cards.use: must know what breaks if a source column is renamed
not: is a list of who viewed the report

cards.subject: A data contract
says: is an agreement on the shape and meaning of data a producer provides
lets consumers rely on a stable schema
is checked automatically when the producer changes
cards.use: want producers to stop breaking downstream reports with silent changes
not: is a legal contract with a customer

cards.subject: Schema drift
says: is an unplanned change in the structure of incoming data
breaks pipelines that assume fixed columns
is caught by schema checks at load time
cards.use: find that a source added a column and the load fails
not: is a planned and announced migration

cards.subject: GROUP BY
says: collapses rows into one row per distinct combination of the listed columns
is needed to pair an aggregate with a plain column
runs after WHERE has filtered rows
cards.use: want revenue per country
not: sorts the output without changing the row count

cards.subject: WHERE
says: filters individual rows before they are grouped
cannot use an aggregate result directly
makes the query read fewer rows
cards.use: want to keep only this year's orders before counting
not: filters groups after aggregation

cards.subject: HAVING
says: filters groups after aggregation
can use an aggregate such as COUNT(*) > 5
applies to grouped results, not raw rows
cards.use: want only customers with more than five orders
not: filters raw rows before grouping

cards.subject: COUNT(*)
says: counts every row in the group, including those with nulls
returns the number of rows rather than values
cards.use: want the number of orders per customer
not: skips rows where any column is null

cards.subject: COUNT(DISTINCT column)
says: counts each different non-null value once
is used to count unique customers rather than orders
is slower than a plain count on big tables
cards.use: want unique buyers rather than total purchases
not: counts every row including repeats

cards.subject: AVG
says: divides the sum by the number of non-null values
ignores null values rather than treating them as zero
is pulled upwards by a few very large values
cards.use: want the mean order value
not: counts nulls as zero

cards.subject: A join fan-out
says: happens when a join matches one row to many and multiplies rows
inflates sums and counts if aggregated afterwards
is avoided by aggregating to the right grain before joining
cards.use: find revenue doubled after joining orders to line items
not: only occurs with a LEFT JOIN

cards.subject: A LEFT JOIN
says: keeps every row from the left table
fills columns from the right table with nulls when no match exists
is used to find rows with no related record
cards.use: want every customer listed, even those with no orders
not: drops rows from the left table without a match

cards.subject: A window function
says: computes across related rows without collapsing them
keeps each input row in the output
is used for running totals and rankings
cards.use: want each order shown alongside its customer's running total
not: collapses rows like GROUP BY

cards.subject: PARTITION BY
says: splits rows into groups inside a window function
restarts the calculation for each group
does not reduce the number of rows
cards.use: want a rank that restarts for each region
not: is another name for GROUP BY

cards.subject: Conditional aggregation
says: puts a CASE expression inside an aggregate
lets one query produce several filtered totals as columns
is used for pivot-style summaries
cards.use: want paid and refunded totals side by side per month
not: requires a separate query for each total

cards.subject: A CTE
says: names a subquery with WITH so it can be read top to bottom
breaks a long query into understandable steps
can be referenced more than once in the same query
cards.use: want to make a nested query readable
not: permanently stores its result as a table

cards.subject: A funnel
says: measures how many users complete each ordered step of a journey
shows the share lost between one step and the next
needs the steps defined in a fixed order
cards.use: want to see where signups are lost between landing and payment
not: groups users by when they joined

cards.subject: A conversion rate
says: is the share of a starting group that completes a goal
needs a clear denominator and time window
can be reported for a single step or the whole funnel
cards.use: want the share of visitors who buy
not: is the raw count of purchases

cards.subject: Drop-off
says: is the share of users lost between two funnel steps
points to the step most worth investigating
is the complement of the step's conversion
cards.use: want to find the step where most people leave
not: is the number who completed the final step

cards.subject: A cohort
says: is a group of users who share a starting point such as signup month
is followed over time as a group
lets groups from different dates be compared fairly
cards.use: want to compare the January signups with the February signups
not: is any random sample of the user base

cards.subject: A segment
says: is a group defined by a trait such as plan, country or device
can be compared on any metric at one point in time
is not tied to a shared start date
cards.use: want to compare mobile users with desktop users
not: is a group that all joined in the same week

cards.subject: A retention table
says: lays out cohorts as rows and time since start as columns
shows the share of each cohort still active at each step
reveals whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones
cards.use: want to see if retention is improving for recent signups
not: lists every user's last login

cards.subject: A retention curve
says: plots the share of a cohort still active against time since start
flattens when a stable core of users stays
falling steadily to zero signals no lasting value
cards.use: want to know if a cohort settles into regular use
not: plots daily revenue over the calendar

cards.subject: Attribution
says: assigns credit for a conversion to the touchpoints before it
gives different answers under different rules such as last touch
is a model, not a measured fact
cards.use: want to decide which channel earned a signup
not: measures exactly what caused the purchase

cards.subject: Activation
says: is the first moment a user gets real value from the product
is defined as a specific early action
often predicts whether a user is retained
cards.use: want to measure whether new users reach their first useful outcome
not: is the moment a user signs up

cards.subject: An A/B test
says: compares two versions by randomly splitting users between them
measures a chosen metric in each group
tests whether a change caused a difference
cards.use: want evidence that a new design really improves signups
not: compares this month with last month

cards.subject: A control group
says: receives the unchanged experience
provides the baseline to compare against
is split from the test group at random
cards.use: need a baseline to judge a change against
not: is chosen as the users most likely to convert

cards.subject: Randomisation
says: assigns users to groups by chance
makes the groups alike apart from the change
is what lets a difference be attributed to the change
cards.use: want to be sure the groups differ only by the change
not: lets users pick the version they prefer

cards.subject: A primary metric
says: is the one measure chosen before the test to decide the result
prevents picking whichever number looks best afterwards
is stated alongside the planned sample size
cards.use: want to decide the winning measure before looking at results
not: is whichever metric moved the most

cards.subject: Sample size planning
says: fixes how many users are needed before the test starts
depends on baseline rate, effect size and desired power
stops a test being ended when results first look good
cards.use: must decide how long to run a test before it starts
not: is decided after seeing the data

cards.subject: Statistical power
says: is the chance of detecting a real effect of a given size
rises with a larger sample
is low in underpowered tests, which miss real effects
cards.use: worry that a small test might miss a real improvement
not: is the chance of a false positive

cards.subject: A p-value
says: is the probability of results at least this extreme if there were no real effect
is not the probability that the change works
is compared with a threshold chosen in advance
cards.use: want to know how surprising the result is if nothing changed
not: is the chance that the hypothesis is true

cards.subject: A confidence interval
says: gives a range of plausible values for the true effect
shows the size and uncertainty together
includes zero when the effect is not clearly different from none
cards.use: want to see how big the lift might really be
not: is the probability the result was a fluke

cards.subject: Peeking
says: is checking results repeatedly and stopping when they look significant
raises the false-positive rate well above the stated level
is avoided by fixing the sample size or using sequential methods
cards.use: see a test turn significant on day three of a planned fourteen
not: makes results more reliable

cards.subject: A multiple-comparisons problem
says: arises when many metrics or variants are tested at once
raises the chance that something looks significant by luck
calls for a stricter threshold or a correction
cards.use: test twenty metrics and find one with a low p-value
not: lowers the chance of a false positive

cards.subject: A sample ratio mismatch
says: is a split of users that differs from the planned allocation
signals a bug in assignment or tracking
means the result should not be trusted until explained
cards.use: find a planned 50/50 test with 52 percent in one group
not: is expected random variation that can be ignored

cards.subject: A novelty effect
says: is a short-lived change in behaviour because something is new
fades as users get used to the change
is a reason to run a test long enough to see it settle
cards.use: see a big lift in the first days that shrinks later
not: is a permanent change in user preference

cards.subject: Practical significance
says: asks whether an effect is big enough to matter
can be absent even when a result is statistically significant
is judged against cost and business value
cards.use: find a significant lift of a tiny fraction of a percent
not: is the same as a low p-value

cards.subject: The mean
says: adds the values and divides by how many there are
is pulled towards very large or very small values
uses every value in the data
cards.use: want the average of a roughly symmetric set of numbers
not: is the middle value when sorted

cards.subject: The median
says: is the middle value when the data is sorted
is barely moved by a few extreme values
is a better summary of typical income than the mean
cards.use: want a typical value that a few huge orders cannot distort
not: is the most frequent value

cards.subject: Variance
says: is the average squared distance from the mean
describes how spread out the values are
is measured in squared units
cards.use: want to know how spread out response times are
not: is the middle value of the data

cards.subject: Standard deviation
says: is the square root of the variance
is in the same units as the data
is small when values cluster near the mean
cards.use: want a spread measure in the same units as the data
not: is the average of the data

cards.subject: A percentile
says: is the value below which a given share of the data falls
describes the tail of a distribution such as the 95th
is how response-time targets are often stated
cards.use: want to know how slow the slowest five percent of requests are
not: is the same as the mean

cards.subject: Correlation
says: measures how strongly two variables move together
ranges from minus one to plus one
does not show that one causes the other
cards.use: want to know whether two measures rise and fall together
not: proves one variable causes the other

cards.subject: Causation
says: means a change in one thing produces a change in another
is best shown by a randomised experiment
cannot be read from correlation alone
cards.use: want to know if a feature actually raised retention
not: is shown by two lines moving together

cards.subject: A confounder
says: is a hidden factor that affects both variables being compared
can create a correlation with no causal link
is controlled by randomisation
cards.use: find that ice cream sales and drownings rise together
not: is a variable that has no effect on anything

cards.subject: Sampling bias
says: occurs when the sample does not represent the population
is created by how people are chosen or who responds
cannot be fixed by making the sample larger
cards.use: survey only customers who contact support and generalise
not: is cured by collecting more of the same responses

cards.subject: Random sampling
says: gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection
avoids systematic bias in who is chosen
makes the sample representative on average
cards.use: want a survey that fairly represents all customers
not: picks the most convenient people

cards.subject: A larger sample
says: shrinks sampling uncertainty
cuts the standard error in proportion to the square root of its size
has diminishing returns once it is already large
cards.use: wonder whether doubling a large sample halves the error
not: remove bias as the sample grows

cards.subject: The central limit theorem
says: says sample means tend towards a normal distribution as samples grow
holds even when the underlying data is not normal
underpins many standard significance tests
cards.use: wonder why means of skewed data can still use normal-based tests
not: says all data is normally distributed

cards.subject: Regression to the mean
says: is the tendency of extreme results to be followed by more typical ones
can make a change seem to work when it did nothing
is a trap when you act on the worst performers
cards.use: see the worst stores improve next month without any action
not: shows a treatment must have worked

cards.subject: Simpson's paradox
says: is a trend that reverses when groups are combined
arises when group sizes differ across categories
is a reason to check segments before trusting a total
cards.use: find each region improved yet the overall rate fell
not: is a mistake in the arithmetic

cards.subject: An outlier
says: is a value far from the rest of the data
can distort the mean but barely moves the median
should be investigated before it is removed
cards.use: find one order a hundred times larger than the rest
not: should always be deleted

cards.subject: A bar chart
says: compares values across categories using bar length
should start its axis at zero
is easy to read for ranking
cards.use: want to compare revenue across regions
not: is best for showing a trend over many dates

cards.subject: A line chart
says: shows how a value changes over ordered time
makes trends and turning points easy to see
joins points to show continuity
cards.use: want to show weekly signups over a year
not: is best for comparing unrelated categories

cards.subject: A scatter plot
says: plots two numeric variables as points
reveals correlation, clusters and outliers
needs no category on either axis
cards.use: want to see whether spend and revenue move together
not: shows part of a whole

cards.subject: A histogram
says: groups a numeric variable into ranges and counts each
shows the shape of a distribution
differs from a bar chart because its bars touch in order
cards.use: want to see how order values are distributed
not: compares unrelated categories

cards.subject: A box plot
says: shows median, quartiles and outliers in one compact shape
compares the spread of several groups side by side
hides the fine shape of the distribution
cards.use: want to compare the spread of delivery times across carriers
not: shows only the mean

cards.subject: A pie chart
says: shows parts of a single whole
becomes hard to read with many slices
makes small differences between slices hard to see
cards.use: want to show a share when there are only two or three parts
not: is the clearest way to compare many categories

cards.subject: A stacked bar chart
says: splits each bar into parts of a whole
makes the bottom segment easy to compare but others hard
shows totals and composition together
cards.use: want totals per month and the mix inside each
not: is ideal for comparing the middle segments

cards.subject: A heatmap
says: shows magnitude using colour across a grid
suits patterns across two categories such as day and hour
is also how cohort retention tables are often drawn
cards.use: want to spot busy hours across the days of a week
not: is best for exact value reading

cards.subject: A truncated axis
says: starts a bar chart's axis above zero
exaggerates small differences
is a common way charts mislead
cards.use: notice a bar chart whose axis starts at 95
not: is recommended to make bars comparable

cards.subject: A dual-axis chart
says: plots two measures on separate vertical scales
lets the apparent relationship change with the chosen scales
can mislead by implying a link
cards.use: see two lines crossing only because the axes were scaled to cross
not: is the safest way to show unrelated data

cards.subject: A logarithmic scale
says: spaces values by ratio rather than by difference
suits data that spans several orders of magnitude
needs a clear label so readers know it is not linear
cards.use: want to show growth from hundreds to millions on one chart
not: makes equal steps mean equal differences

cards.subject: ETL
says: extracts data, transforms it, then loads the result into the destination
does the cleaning before the data reaches the warehouse
was common when warehouse storage was expensive
cards.use: need to clean and reshape data before it lands in the target
not: loads raw data first and transforms afterwards

cards.subject: ELT
says: loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there
keeps the raw copy so transformations can be rerun
uses the warehouse's own compute for the transformation
cards.use: want to keep raw data and reshape it later in the warehouse
not: transforms data before loading

cards.subject: A data warehouse
says: stores structured, cleaned data organised for analysis
is built for large read queries rather than many small writes
holds history from many source systems
cards.use: want one place to query data from many systems
not: is built for fast single-row updates in an app

cards.subject: A data lake
says: stores raw data of many formats at low cost
applies structure when the data is read
can become unusable without a catalog
cards.use: need cheap storage for raw files before deciding how to use them
not: enforces a strict schema before loading

cards.subject: An OLAP system
says: answers analytical queries that scan and aggregate large data
is organised for reading many rows of a few columns
stores data in a column-oriented layout in many products
cards.use: need to aggregate a year of events quickly
not: handles individual order inserts for the app

cards.subject: Batch processing
says: processes data in groups on a schedule
is simpler and cheaper than streaming
adds delay between an event and its result
cards.use: need a nightly rebuild of daily totals
not: processes each event the instant it arrives

cards.subject: Stream processing
says: processes each event soon after it arrives
gives low-latency results
is harder to run correctly than batch
cards.use: need live fraud signals within seconds
not: waits for the end of the day

cards.subject: Orchestration
says: schedules pipeline steps and runs them in dependency order
retries failed steps and raises alerts
makes it clear what ran and when
cards.use: need step B to run only after step A succeeds
not: transforms the data itself

cards.subject: An idempotent pipeline
says: gives the same result however many times it is run
makes safe retries and reruns possible
is built by replacing a partition or using upserts rather than appending blindly
cards.use: need to rerun yesterday's load without duplicating rows
not: adds the same rows again on every rerun

cards.subject: A fact table
says: records measurable events such as orders, one row per event
holds numeric measures and keys to dimensions
is usually the largest table in a model
cards.use: want a table of every sale with its amount
not: lists descriptive attributes like customer name

cards.subject: A dimension table
says: holds descriptive attributes such as customer or product
is joined to a fact table to slice measures
is smaller and changes more slowly than facts
cards.use: want to group sales by product category
not: records every transaction

cards.subject: A star schema
says: places one fact table in the centre joined to dimension tables
makes analytical queries simple and fast
denormalises dimensions to reduce joins
cards.use: want an easy model for slicing sales by many attributes
not: normalises every attribute into many linked tables

cards.subject: A backfill
says: reprocesses historical data after a fix or a new definition
should be repeatable and not duplicate rows
can change reported numbers for past periods
cards.use: need to recompute last year's totals after changing a metric
not: is a live stream of new events

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects only the data needed for the stated purpose
reduces what can leak or be misused
is a principle of privacy law such as GDPR
cards.use: are asked to add a field 'just in case'
not: says collect everything that might be useful

cards.subject: Pseudonymisation
says: replaces direct identifiers with a code
keeps data linkable if the key is held separately
still counts as personal data
cards.use: want to analyse behaviour without showing names
not: makes data fully anonymous

cards.subject: Anonymisation
says: removes the ability to identify any individual
cannot be reversed by reasonable means
takes data out of the scope of personal data rules when done properly
cards.use: want to share data that no longer identifies anyone
not: is just removing the name column

cards.subject: Consent
says: is a clear, specific agreement given before data is collected
can be withdrawn by the person
must be recorded as evidence
cards.use: need a legal basis for non-essential tracking
not: is assumed if the user keeps browsing

cards.subject: A retention limit
says: sets how long data is kept
requires deletion when the period ends
is stated in a policy and enforced by jobs
cards.use: want old event data removed automatically
not: means data is kept forever by default

cards.subject: Minimum group size
says: hides results from groups smaller than a set number
stops small counts revealing an individual
is applied in reports that slice data finely
cards.use: want a breakdown that cannot expose one person
not: shows every group however small

cards.subject: Purpose limitation
says: restricts use of data to the purposes it was collected for
needs fresh consent for a new, incompatible use
is a reason to document why each field is held
cards.use: want to reuse support data for marketing analysis
not: allows any reuse once data is collected

cards.subject: Access control for data
says: limits who can see which fields and datasets
follows least privilege
should be logged so access can be audited
cards.use: need analysts to see only what their job needs
not: gives every analyst the whole warehouse

cards.subject: The right to erasure
says: lets a person ask for their personal data to be deleted
has to reach copies in analytics stores and backups per policy
is harder when data is spread across many systems
cards.use: receive a request to delete a user's data
not: applies only to the main application database

cards.subject: The Moksy token ledger
says: records user, organisation, project, provider, model, token counts, estimated cost, billing period and request id for every AI completion
is append-only, with corrections as reversing entries
sits beside a fast summary snapshot held on the subscription
cards.use: need a durable record of each AI completion for billing and limits
not: keeps token usage in memory only and loses it on restart

cards.subject: Usage service versus billing truth in Moksy
says: treats the usage service as product analytics and quota telemetry
keeps billing truth in the subscriptions ledger
needs the money source to be append-only, idempotent and reconciled
cards.use: must decide which Moksy store is the source of truth for money
not: makes the dashboard-tuned usage store the billing record

cards.subject: Moksy quota reserve and commit
says: reserves quota before the provider call
commits the actual usage afterwards
stops concurrent requests overspending the allowance
cards.use: need concurrent AI requests not to exceed a customer's quota
not: checks the limit only after the provider call finishes

cards.subject: The mid-month reset bug
says: advanced the next reset from the wrong date
let one allowance run for two months
shows why period dates need careful computation and tests
cards.use: hear of an allowance that lasted twice as long as intended
not: blocked customers a month too early

cards.subject: The Moksy exportable field registry
says: is defined in code per resource
keeps any field not declared exportable inside the database
stops fields that are not importable from ever being written
cards.use: want to be sure a new column does not leak through export
not: exports every column unless it is blocked afterwards

cards.subject: Moksy import dry run
says: shows a diff of what an import would change before applying it
can produce rollback operations
lets a person check the effect before committing
cards.use: want to see what an import changes before it runs
not: applies the import immediately with no preview

cards.subject: CSV injection
says: happens when exported text starting with equals, plus, minus or at is read as a formula
is fixed by neutralising such leading characters in exported cells
was raised in GG Money's stress run for bank-supplied text
cards.use: export bank-supplied text that a spreadsheet may execute
not: is prevented by exporting as a larger file

cards.subject: GG Money plan history
says: ends the old plan line and starts a new one when an amount changes
keeps last quarter judged against last quarter's plan
lets variance stay honest over time
cards.use: change a planned amount without rewriting past reports
not: overwrites the old amount in place

cards.subject: An unplanned posting in GG Money
says: is a posting that no plan line claims
is shown as unplanned and never dropped, so totals still reconcile
makes surprise spending visible
cards.use: find spending that matches no plan line
not: is hidden from the report to keep it tidy

cards.subject: The all-companies view in GG Money
says: leaves out sales between the owner's own companies
avoids counting the same money twice
is needed so combined totals are not inflated
cards.use: combine the owner's companies into one total
not: adds intercompany sales in so revenue looks larger

cards.subject: A frozen review in GG Money
says: freezes a period with a fingerprint
needs a second person to approve
makes later changes to a reviewed period detectable
cards.use: want a closed period that cannot be altered unnoticed
not: can be edited freely by the person who prepared it

qa.q: Which statistic is least affected by a few extremely large values?
qa.right: The median
qa.why: The median depends on position in the sorted data, not on how large the extremes are.

qa.q: What does a funnel report show?
qa.right: The share of users who complete each ordered step of a journey
wrong: The average time between two logins
The list of users who share a birthday
qa.why: A funnel tracks drop-off from one step to the next.

qa.q: Why write down the definition of an active user?
qa.right: So every team computes the same number from the same data
wrong: So the number always goes up
So the data needs no cleaning
So events can be deleted sooner
qa.why: Without a shared definition, different teams report different figures.

qa.q: Which chart suits showing weekly signups across a year?
qa.right: A line chart
qa.why: Line charts show change over ordered time.

qa.q: Which of these best describes correlation?
qa.right: Two variables tend to move together
wrong: One variable is proved to cause the other
qa.why: Correlation describes association, not cause.

qa.q: Which query returns the number of orders per customer?
qa.right: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
wrong: SELECT COUNT(customer_id) FROM orders WHERE customer_id;
SELECT customer_id FROM orders HAVING COUNT(*);
qa.why: Pairing a plain column with an aggregate needs GROUP BY on that column.

qa.q: What does this query count?
qa.right: The distinct buyers who ordered, each counted once
wrong: Every order row in the table
The orders placed by the first customer
qa.why: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts each different non-null value once.

qa.q: A table has 100 rows and 20 of them have a null email. What does COUNT(email) return?
qa.why: COUNT(column) skips nulls, COUNT(*) does not.

qa.q: What does AVG(score) do with rows where score is null?
qa.right: Ignores them
wrong: Treats them as the previous value
qa.why: Aggregate functions skip nulls, so the average is over non-null values only.

qa.q: Why is an event ID useful?
qa.right: A retried delivery can be recognised and counted once
wrong: It makes the event faster to send
It removes the need for a timestamp
qa.why: A unique id lets a duplicate be detected.

qa.q: Which filter belongs in HAVING rather than WHERE?
qa.right: Customers with more than five orders
qa.why: The count exists only after grouping, so it must be filtered with HAVING.
qa.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

qa.q: What is the aim of randomising users in an A/B test?
qa.right: To make the groups alike apart from the change being tested
wrong: To make the test finish sooner
To ensure the new version wins
To give every user both versions
qa.why: Random assignment spreads other differences evenly across groups.

qa.q: What does a tracking plan hold?
qa.right: The events and properties to send, with their meaning and owner
wrong: The passwords for the analytics tool
The list of customers who opted out
qa.why: A tracking plan is the agreed contract for event data.

qa.q: Which chart type should normally start its axis at zero?
qa.right: A bar chart
wrong: A line chart showing a small change
qa.why: Bar length encodes value, so a truncated axis misleads.

qa.q: Which is a leading indicator for subscription renewals?
qa.right: Whether new customers complete their first useful action
wrong: Total cancellations in the closed quarter
qa.why: Early behaviour moves before the renewal outcome.

qa.q: What is the best reason to use a data warehouse for reporting rather than the live app database?
qa.right: It is organised for large analytical queries without slowing the app
wrong: It is faster for single-row updates
It stores only the latest values
qa.why: Analytical scans and live transactions suit different designs.

qa.q: A dashboard shows revenue of 1.2m but finance says 1.0m. What should you do first?
qa.right: Compare both definitions and reconcile each to the source data
wrong: Replace the dashboard with finance's spreadsheet
Hide the dashboard until next quarter
qa.why: A mismatch usually comes from different definitions, filters or periods.

qa.q: A team joins orders to order lines and sums order totals. The total doubles. Why?
qa.right: The join repeats each order once per line, so its total is added several times
wrong: The orders table has null totals
The join sorted the rows incorrectly
qa.why: A one-to-many join fans out rows, inflating sums taken at the order level.

qa.q: A variant shows a 3 percent lift with p = 0.04 after the team checked results daily for two weeks and stopped when it first dipped below 0.05. What is the concern?
qa.right: Repeated peeking inflates the false-positive rate, so the p-value overstates the evidence
wrong: A p-value below 0.05 is never valid
Two weeks is too short for any test
Daily checks reduce the sample size
qa.why: Stopping at the first significant look breaks the test's stated error rate.

qa.q: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. What is the most likely explanation?
qa.right: A common cause, hot weather, drives both
qa.why: A confounder can produce correlation with no causal link.

qa.q: A survey of customers who contacted support finds 60 percent are unhappy. What can you conclude about all customers?
qa.right: Very little, because the sample is not representative
wrong: 60 percent of all customers are unhappy
The sample is large enough to ignore bias
qa.why: Sampling bias is not fixed by sample size.

qa.q: Average order value is 80 and the median is 35. What does this suggest?
qa.right: A few very large orders pull the mean up, so the distribution is skewed
wrong: The mean and median should always match
qa.why: Mean above median points to a right-skewed distribution.

qa.q: What does a 95 percent confidence interval of -0.5 to +4.0 percentage points for a lift tell you?
qa.right: The true effect could be zero or slightly negative, so the result is inconclusive
wrong: The test needs no further consideration
qa.why: An interval that includes zero does not show a clear difference.

qa.q: A retry sends a usage event twice. Which design prevents double counting?
qa.right: Store a unique key per request and ignore a write whose key already exists
wrong: Sum all events and halve the result
Delete the second event by hand each day
qa.why: Idempotent writes make retries safe.

qa.q: Which statement about a p-value is correct?
qa.right: It is the probability of results this extreme if there were no real effect
wrong: It is the probability the change works
It is the size of the effect
It is the chance the test was run correctly
qa.why: A p-value assumes the null hypothesis and measures surprise.

qa.q: A pie chart with twelve slices is hard to read. What is a better choice?
qa.right: A sorted bar chart
wrong: A pie chart with brighter colours
qa.why: Bars make comparison across many categories easy.

qa.q: Why keep raw data in an ELT pipeline?
qa.right: Transformations can be changed and rerun without reloading from the source
wrong: It uses less storage than cleaned data
It removes the need for a warehouse
qa.why: Raw data lets definitions evolve.

qa.q: A report exports user emails to a partner who only needs counts. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Export aggregated counts and leave out the email column
wrong: Keep emails but zip the file
Ask the partner to delete emails later
qa.why: Data minimisation avoids sending data that is not needed.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a data quality problem?
qa.right: A chart using a clear title
qa.why: A chart title is presentation, not data quality.

qa.q: A cohort table shows later cohorts retain better each month. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Product or onboarding changes may be improving retention
wrong: Retention cannot be compared across cohorts
qa.why: Comparing cohorts at the same age shows whether retention is improving.

qa.q: A late event for last Tuesday arrives today. How should a well-designed pipeline treat it?
qa.right: Assign it to Tuesday by event time and reprocess that day's total
qa.why: Event time decides the period, so recent windows are reprocessed.

qa.q: A test planned 50/50 shows 10,400 users in A and 9,600 in B. What should you do?
qa.right: Investigate a possible sample ratio mismatch before trusting any result
wrong: Remove users from A until it is even
qa.why: A split that differs from plan indicates an assignment or tracking fault.

qa.q: A growth team tests 20 metrics and ships because one reached p = 0.03. What is the problem?
qa.right: With many comparisons, one such result is likely by chance alone
wrong: P-values are not used in tests
qa.why: Multiple comparisons need a stricter threshold or a pre-chosen primary metric.

qa.q: A cheap model downgrade is added when users reach their limit. Which metric should guard it?
qa.right: Customer satisfaction or cancellations after the downgrade
qa.why: A guardrail checks the change does not harm customers.

qa.q: Two requests arrive together when 10 units of quota remain, each needing 8. How does reserving first help?
qa.right: The first reserves 8, so the second is refused or reduced instead of overspending
wrong: Both succeed and the ledger fixes it later
The second waits until the month ends
qa.why: Reservation makes concurrent checks see the same remaining balance.

qa.q: A wrong 500-unit entry sits in an append-only usage ledger. How is it corrected?
qa.right: Add a reversing entry of minus 500, then the right entry
wrong: Reset the total by hand in the snapshot
qa.why: Append-only ledgers keep history and correct with new rows.

qa.q: Each of two regions improved its conversion rate, yet the overall rate fell. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: A shift in traffic towards the region with the lower rate, Simpson's paradox
wrong: An arithmetic error that can only be a bug
qa.why: Mix changes can reverse the combined trend.

qa.q: Which design lets an analyst filter on the meaning they understand when an event's field changes?
qa.right: Add a version to the event and keep the old version's meaning
wrong: Rename the field without telling anyone
qa.why: Versioning avoids silently mixing meanings.

qa.q: A pipeline loads a day's data by appending. It fails halfway and is rerun. What is the risk?
qa.right: Duplicate rows for the part that loaded the first time
qa.why: Appending is not idempotent; replacing the partition is.

qa.q: What does this query produce?
qa.right: Each order with a running total per customer, by date
wrong: Only the latest order per customer
qa.why: A window function keeps rows and computes across a partition.

qa.q: The worst-performing stores each improve next month with no intervention. What explains it?
qa.right: Regression to the mean
qa.why: Extreme results tend to move toward typical ones.

qa.q: A test is stopped after one week with a 12 percent lift. Two weeks later the lift is 2 percent. What may have occurred?
qa.right: A novelty effect faded as users got used to the change
wrong: The lift was caused by the p-value
qa.why: Early lifts from novelty often shrink.

qa.q: An export includes a cell with =HYPERLINK(...) from bank-supplied text. What is the risk?
qa.right: A spreadsheet may treat it as a formula, which is CSV injection
qa.why: Cells starting with = + - or @ can execute in spreadsheets.

qa.q: A feature's users retain better than non-users. Can you say the feature improves retention?
qa.right: No, users who choose it may already be more engaged, so a randomised test is needed
wrong: Yes, if the sample is large
qa.why: Self-selection confounds the comparison.

qa.q: You report a metric to a team that is paid on it. Over time the metric improves but customer complaints rise. Which idea explains this?
qa.right: Goodhart's law: a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
qa.why: People optimise the target rather than the goal.

qa.q: A test of a rare outcome is underpowered and shows no significant effect. What is the sound conclusion?
qa.right: The test could not detect an effect of that size, so the question is still open
wrong: The p-value proves the null hypothesis
qa.why: Not significant is not the same as no effect.

qa.q: A rare condition affects 1 in 1,000 people and a test is 99 percent accurate. A person tests positive. What matters most for the true chance they have it?
qa.right: The base rate, since most positives will be false
qa.why: A low base rate means false positives dominate.

qa.q: A report with a 98 percent match between two systems still hides what risk?
qa.right: The 2 percent mismatch may be concentrated in the most valuable records
qa.why: Look at where the differences fall, not just how many.

qa.q: A consent record is withdrawn. Which action is most consistent with good practice?
qa.right: Stop collecting, and delete or de-identify the person's analytics data per policy
wrong: Keep collecting until the next quarter
Keep all data but hide it from dashboards
Ask the person to sign again
qa.why: Withdrawal must be honoured going forward and in held data as policy requires.

qa.q: A small region breakdown shows two users. Why might this report be a privacy risk?
qa.right: A group that small can reveal what one person did
wrong: Two is not a valid number
qa.why: A minimum group size prevents re-identification.

qa.q: Which choice best shows a trend and a precise value together on a KPI tile?
qa.right: The number with a small sparkline and the change against the previous period
wrong: A pie chart of the number
qa.why: Context turns a bare number into information.

qa.q: Which type of tracking is the safer source for a completed payment?
qa.right: Server-side tracking after the payment succeeds
qa.why: Server-side events reflect what really happened and avoid ad-blockers.

qa.q: What is the main difference between a cohort and a segment?
qa.right: A cohort shares a start point and is followed over time, while a segment shares a trait
qa.why: Cohort analysis is about time since a shared starting event.

qa.q: Why can a 99th percentile response time be more useful than the mean?
qa.right: It shows how slow the worst requests are, which the mean hides
wrong: It is always lower than the mean
It removes the need for monitoring
qa.why: Tails drive user pain, and means blur them.

qa.q: A dashboard needs yesterday's figures to be final by 8am. Late events keep arriving for two days. What is a sound design?
qa.right: Reprocess a rolling window of recent days and mark recent figures as provisional
wrong: Freeze the day at midnight forever
qa.why: Provisional labelling plus reprocessing keeps numbers honest.
